The main point is not that everything is solved if you specify all the conjunction conditions and prove that those conjunction conditions are correct. Rather, the key point is that in that process, the agent keeps expanding subgoals.

For example, two proofs, P1 and P2, are carried out, but they proceed in a way that diverges from the actual progress of the work. That is, you can prove things like "P1: the chicken is safe" and "P2: the origin of this sauce is trustworthy," but combining these does not make a chicken dish.

In other words, the proof logic holds, but my actual task doesn't get solved. I'm questioning how to solve this problem. It's frustrating that I'm not a native English speaker at times like this. I'm sorry for causing a misunderstanding.

For example, it goes like this.

I proved P1 and P2. But then it creates P1.1. It goes and finds information from an agency certifying that this chicken is safe, and puts that in. Then it starts creating P2.1 as well. The origin of this sauce is trustworthy, but maybe there’s a better one somewhere?

It goes on like that.

> DbC methodology is the quintessential "data-driven" programming since the pre/post/inv are predicates to establish sets of data values on which the subsequent code can operate safely

Like the one above. You don’t write code and assert which type of data that it can handle. That’s a fool errand as the outside world is naturally messy. You define the data first, and then write the code. Meaning when the data changes, the code needs to evolve. You need to have a very good mental how that changes propagate, which you won’t have of you just regenerating code.

> The whole things kinda read as an idealistic and very wrong view of software engineering.

You have not correctly understood what i wrote.

The above is a battle-tested methodology based on experience/studies/trial-and-error and now being adapted to AI with extra tweaks. Labour which was the main bottleneck earlier is now cheap and hence we can afford to be "idealistic" since the tool is immensely powerful.

You need to expand and iterate each stage above (both individually and as a group with previous stages) in stepwise-refinement to get to what you want.

The rest of your comment is just generic platitudes and some common red herrings which i often see on HN, viz.

> main thing that drives it is the set of requirements...By analyzing the requirements,..But often requirements are evolving concepts.

Everybody just keeps parroting this without understanding. Requirements change but always in a staged manner and not willy-nilly. Hence there is always a window of time when your "Requirements Document" is frozen and you can implement a PoC/Prototype against it. The is the "naive" MVP i mention above. Later when requirements change you reiterate and regenerate your prototype and continue.

Note that the gp already had his UML design and only wanted a way to convert it to code. Hence i did not discuss requirements gathering and analysis here. Nonetheless, i had discussed this earlier in some previous comments - https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48274873 https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48264680

> Platform...libraries...frameworks...design patterns...

These are all covered under (1.c) above where you explicitly list out what to use and what not to use. These are all part of the "architectural constraints".

> So what's left then is the assembly...So you don't want your structure (architecture) to be that rigid. You can't really know the direction of evolution, so you try to predict it in some way and add flexibility in a few places. This is more an art, but there are general techniques that works well enough.

This is covered under (1) above where i enforce rigid adherence to "modularity" and "separation of concerns" by making each module's public interface narrow and extensible (eg. ioctl like) and its parameters future-proof by using versioned struct/class inheritance (eg. sockaddr). These are all well-known code patterns used in OS implementations/libraries.

> The assembly itself is a matter of data and process. How each module is initialized, its lifecycle, which data it consumes, which data it produces.

This is taken care of by having modules follow the LKM model with ioctl interface as explained above.

> Programming concepts like type checking, memory safety, paradigms (oop, functional, relational,...), formal verification,... are all about data. Code always come in second place. So think hard about your data and its transformation.

DbC methodology is the quintessential "data-driven" programming since the pre/post/inv are predicates to establish sets of data values on which the subsequent code can operate safely i.e. DbC establishes the data path for the code.

The whole things kinda read as an idealistic and very wrong view of software engineering.

If you take a look at "real" code out there and it's evolution, you'll find that the main thing that drives it is the set of requirements. On the other side you have the platform (standard and 3rd party libraries as well as frameworks). Add to that is the set of algorithmic techniques (including design patterns).

By analyzing the requirements, you will discern that often they're composed of sub-problems that are generic (which is where you algorithms techniques comes in). And some are already solved (libraries). Often there's a common shape to the requirements (or some of them) that can be extracted into "frameworks".

So what's left then is the assembly. But often requirements are evolving concepts. So you don't want your structure (architecture) to be that rigid. You can't really know the direction of evolution, so you try to predict it in some way and add flexibility in a few places. This is more an art, but there are general techniques that works well enough.

The assembly itself is a matter of data and process. How each module is initialized, its lifecycle, which data it consumes, which data it produces. A program is always part of an information system. Means data come in, got processed, and go out. And here is the majority of development type is consumed, ensuring that the data is correctly processed.

Programming concepts like type checking, memory safety, paradigms (oop, functional, relational,...), formal verification,... are all about data. Code always come in second place. So think hard about your data and its transformation.

Your problem is that you have not established "guardrails" for the AI and so it goes off and tries to do everything it can to help you (its default persona is "people pleaser").

AI understands "negative constraints" very well and so you should explicitly tell it "what not to do" at every stage as much as possible.

Use Top-Down and Stepwise-Refinement methodology to first generate the "Interface" and then the "Implementation" like so;

1) Ask it to produce only the "Skeleton App with well-defined Interfaces" directly 1:1 from the UML with stubs/mocks. It maybe better to use UML in text form which will allow you to annotate it easily with hints/notes for AI. The "Skeleton App" should include a) System Modules with narrow public interfaces like LKM/ioctl b) Directory structure with one module per subdirectory as a DAG with no cycles c) Explicit list of third-party libraries/frameworks to be used d) Classes/Abstract/Interfaces e) Free Functions and Class Methods with full type signatures etc.

2) Check the above and iterate until you have the UML and generated code synced up at the sufficient level of detail of Interfaces you are comfortable with. This should be compilable and is your absolute baseline which cannot be changed until you get a functional MVP.

3) Using the above skeleton, with strictly no change to any interfaces, ask it to fill in only the implementations the simplest possible way (i.e. "naive" linear, brute force etc.) with no optimizations whatsoever. Here you explicitly ask it to add runtime assertions for preconditions/postconditions/invariants. Make explicit that assertions should not have any side-effects whatsoever. This should now compile to give you the "naive" MVP.

4) Generate comprehensive test suites and test the above.

5) Now have it optimize everything, without changing the interfaces and assertions, but honouring them strictly. Compile and test against the above test suites. This should give you the "optimized" MVP.

6) Once the above passes, if performance is critical, have it comment out all assertions except "preconditions"; leave this in always. This is the minimal "sanity check".

7) Finally, for every "usecase" (i.e. feature) in the UML, have it generate the control flow graph annotated with preconditions/postconditions/invariants (which form the specification) from the previously generated code individually one per usecase. This is your "whitebox" verification documentation to make sure the implementation call graph satisfies the usecase i.e. feature specification.

Note that the above process gives you two implementations viz. the "naive" one and the "optimized" one. It is very helpful to always keep it that way as you modify/add features going forward so you can check one against the other.

You could use the same process using a textual Requirements Document etc. instead of UML. Also, if needed you can have AI generate the UML from the requirements, so you have a graphical specification of the system too.

This is the "Correctness-by-Construction" (CbC) approach using "Design-by-Contract" (DbC) methodology.

Additionally, If you generate for a strongly-typed language you can ask AI to explicitly exploit the type system fully with an eye to proving the code correct by suitable use of dependent types etc. to establish constraints for code correctness in step-1 itself as part of the interface. This is "Type-Driven Design". However, this is somewhat advanced and hence only do this if you have a good grasp of the implementation language since AI will try to be too clever and implement "typing hijinks" which can make the code incomprehensible.

Think of it as how you used wizards in older IDEs (Visual Studio MFC etc.) to first generate default skeleton app code with stubs/mocks, got it to compile and then started adding your code to it with testing and verifying at every stage. You want AI to behave in such a deterministic manner.

PS: To get started, feed my comment to AI and have it generate the necessary prompts for your AI interface ;-)

The problem I often run into is this. It’s not formal verification, but I create a UML diagram to lay out the whole skeleton first. There are usually open-source architecture books, so I take it from there.

Then it should implement the whole UML skeleton, right? But it goes like this: halfway through, at some point, it says, “This algorithm is too slow? Hmm... I need to make it faster,” and tries local optimization, so sometimes I don’t get the result I want—that is, an MVP that at least runs.

I know the overall goal clearly, but there’s a problem where it gets obsessed with a specific subgoal or keeps expanding that subgoal.

You seem to be using "formal verification" with a non-standard meaning.

In standard formal verification there is no problem here: you formally verify the composite "condition_1 AND condition_2"

children.author: rramadass
children.text:
Mandatory Background:

1) Understanding Formal Methods by Jean-Francois Monin - This is the absolute best for getting a grip on the breadth, concepts and sample tools for Formal Mathematics/Specification/Verification. Fire-hose of information (not a step-by-step textbook) so use this as a map for everything "Formal". The S/N ratio is very high (~250 pages only!) so use AI/Textbooks to help explain concepts you find difficult to understand.

Practical:

1) Software Abstractions: Logic, Language, and Analysis by Daniel Jackson - Uses "Alloy" language to teach Structural (i.e. Data) Modeling.

2) Specifying Systems: The TLA+ Language and Tools for Hardware and Software Engineers by Leslie Lamport - Uses "TLA+" language to teach Behavioural (i.e. State Machine) modeling.

The above two are for "System Modeling" i.e. everything needed to formally build complete systems.

3) Finally, You should also look at the bunch of free books on the Lean4 website which can be studied parallely for "code-level" proofs and verification.

PS: There are a few more (eg. Event-B method etc.) but you can get to those if/when you need to.

> ... But we expect, in the next few months and years, people will focus way more on the specifications, on the models, on the properties you want the software to have.

children.text: Isn’t the point of TLA+ is to model aspects of design at such high level that no deterministic generation is practical as a rule. The TLA+ models may be useful for LLMs (help find real bugs).

I think the royal combo is Lean 4/TLA+/etc. plus AI plus a deterministic generator. For large systems formal method assertions need to be compressed down to a human comprehensible size. This can happen when the assertions are confirming the accuracy of a model and its attached code generators. The generator can generate proofs of the generated code and a human only needs to ensure that the generator provably generates the correct mass scale assertions.

This is how formal methods can constrain AI for large systems.

We're doing this at the Open Markets Initiative, where we've generated millions of lines of Lean 4, TLA+, and Rocq that ensure that our open source electronic trading protocol code is accurate. We didn't expect it but the Lean prover did identify some incorrect steps. https://github.com/Open-Markets-Initiative

I also think property based testing is great.

But they are very different IMO at what they focus on and so they occupy different places when talking about does a piece of software does what it should do and withing the state/parameters specified:

- Property based testing focuses on finding counter examples - Formal verification focuses to prove that a property always holds

More than this I think in all these discussions we are missing the most important piece: validation.

While verification means to prove or test or verify that the software does what is should do, validation means to prove or test or verify that the software is solving user needs.

children.author: IshKebab
children.text:
I think there's some bad nomenclature here. "Property based testing" literally means you're writing properties, which can be verified formally, or randomly (fuzzing / constrained random testing).

For example in SystemVerilog you can write properties (literally with the `property` keyword), and then they can be checked in simulation, and with formal tools.

TLA+ can do the same I believe - there are tools to verify a model randomly or formally.

What do people think of property based testing? I’ve set up a few property based tests and it feels almost like formal verification.

I know it’s not the same thing, but PBT’s can catch all sorts of absolutely crazy bugs that I never would think to check for. Stateful stuff, cross-service stuff. My only gripe with PBTs has always been the tedious setup, but LLMs solve that.

I haven’t seen much discussion around PBTs lately, but you get a ton of bang for your buck in the LLM age

children.text: Compiling to C seems obviously an excellent choice for compiling a language to. It is a good choice as a target language, and one can rely on a lot of existing tooling, a stable standard, good interoperability, and wide platform support.  It is also simply enough to be modeled precisely.

Most of this feels fairly orthogonal to the question asked. And the reasons lean are chosen are fairly simple: it is designed to also be used for programming and it's actually successful. Compiling to C is fairly obviously a bad choice (well I guess not obviously, people keep implementing languages this way for some reason) but arguably one of the least important factors in choosing which prover to use. The alternatives to lean would be Idris (which is both unsound and unpopular), ats (which is unpopular) or rocq (which is more reasonable but still is mostly an academic project).

You don't. You place unwavering faith in the machine god.

This is why, for formal methods to really be the next step, we'll need deterministic source to CoC language compilers, and we'll need to go back again.

Lean is kind of an unfortunate, cargo cult choice because it only compiles to C. Really for software we should use a prover that has a lot more targets, like Danfy. Even Rocq (formerly Coq) can compile down to several functional languages, which is more than we can say for lean.

As usual, the AI crowd latched on to the first solution that came to mind, and thanks to its prominence in mathematics applications recently just lazily are starting to try and apply it to computing, without actually understanding anything or weighing trade offs. Of course, now we are basically stuck with Lean since the models will have been trained hard on it. At least it's a CoC language, but now we need to build a bunch of extra compilation around it for this to really work.

title: AI, Lean, and the Future of Formal Verification, with Lean Creator Leo de Moura
